title: A Mathematical Shock in a Slack Thread: OpenAI Wants to Put a Speed Limiter on AI Development
excerpt: To OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki, a large model is essentially a compressor: first build a large computer, train a compressor on unstructured data, then
content_html:
To OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki, a large model is essentially a compressor: first build a large computer, train a compressor on unstructured data, then unlock its potential through prompting, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. The yardstick for measuring its progress has not changed in years—perplexity, or how accurately it predicts the next token; the lower the number, the more accurate it is. On November 22, he wrote that this very yardstick should be used to draw a verifiable speed limit for frontier model development.

The night the answers started appearing one after another

Over the past year or so, OpenAI has continued to test models with unsolved math problems. After upgrading to a model with log perplexity of about 0.76, answers to long-standing open math problems unexpectedly appeared one after another in the same Slack thread—something that, for people who do math, “felt very unreal.” Looking back: GPT-3.5 at about 0.99 learned fluent conversation, GPT-4 at about 0.91 could effectively use chain-of-thought, and today, below 0.8, transformative capabilities are already appearing in cybersecurity and math. No one predicted “what would emerge at a given threshold,” which made him wary: once AI participates in algorithm research, pretraining could accelerate abruptly, while progress in alignment and monitoring may not keep up.

A self-consistent red line, with known weaknesses

His proposal took shape from this: use measurements such as perplexity to define the first red line, stating that it must not be crossed before reaching milestones such as “a successor to CoT monitors,” and use it as a general framework for later speed limits. The clever part is its self-consistency—the same metric can both measure progress and set limits. He is also aware of its weak spots: it does not map to specific tasks; chain-of-thought greatly boosts capability without lowering it; no one knows the intrinsic entropy floor of data; and evaluation sets differ from group to group. The real question left is: when the most astonishing progress lies precisely outside the metric, can a single number still contain “intelligence”?
